title: PMP Renewal: How PDUs Actually Work
dek: You need 60 PDUs every three years plus a renewal fee of $60 for PMI members or $150 for non-members. What almost nobody tells you: a large share of those PDUs can be earned without paying for anything, including by doing your own job.

seo.metaTitle: PMP Renewal: How PDUs Actually Work
seo.metaDescription: How to renew your PMP — 60 PDUs over three years, the Talent Triangle minimums, the fee, and why much of it can be earned without paying anything.

sources.label: PMI — How to maintain your certification

body.richText: Passing the PMP isn't the end of the spending. The certification expires every three years, and keeping it requires both a fee and 60 professional development units — PDUs. Plenty of companies will happily sell you a PDU bundle for hundreds of dollars. Before you buy one, here's how the system actually works.

The short version: 60 PDUs every three years, plus a renewal fee of $60 for PMI members or $150 for non-members. Within that 60, you must earn at least 8 PDUs in each of the three PMI Talent Triangle areas. A substantial share of the total can be earned at no cost.

body.caption: PMP renewal requirements (source: PMI; confirm current details in the CCR Handbook).
rows: At least 8 PDUs in each of the 3 areas

body.richText: One PDU generally represents one hour of qualifying learning or contribution. Sixty hours across three years works out to about twenty hours a year — roughly two hours a month. Framed that way it's far less daunting than the number suggests.

body.text: The Talent Triangle, and why it catches people out

body.richText: PMI structures professional development around three skill areas, and you must earn a minimum of 8 PDUs in each:

items: Ways of Working — the technical craft: methods, tools, delivery approaches
Power Skills — leadership, communication, collaboration, dealing with people
Business Acumen — strategy, commercial understanding, how the organization actually works

body.richText: This is where people get stuck near the deadline. It's easy to accumulate PDUs in the area you enjoy — usually technical — and arrive at the end of the cycle short of the 8 required in another. Check your balance per area, not just your total, and check it early.

body.text: The two ways to earn PDUs

body.richText: PMI splits PDUs into two categories, and understanding the difference is what saves you money.

richText: — learning activities. This is the required category, and PMI places no cap on how many PDUs you can earn this way. It includes courses and training, but also a great deal that costs nothing.

— contributing rather than consuming. This is optional, and PMI limits how much of your total can come from it, so treat it as a supplement rather than a strategy. It includes working in your certified role, writing articles or blog posts, giving webinars, creating content, mentoring, teaching, and volunteering.

body.text: How to renew without paying for PDUs

body.richText: This is the part the PDU-bundle sellers would rather you didn't work out. Between free education and giving back, most people can cover the bulk of a cycle at no cost:

items: Working in your certified role — simply practising project management counts as giving back
Free webinars, including PMI's own member resources and chapter events
Reading and self-directed learning that meets PMI's criteria
Mentoring a colleague or teaching what you know
Writing about the profession — articles, posts, or talks
Volunteering with PMI or a local chapter

body.richText: The practical approach: log PDUs as you earn them rather than hunting for 60 in the final month. Late panic is exactly what makes people buy an expensive bundle they didn't need. A note in your calendar every few months is enough.

Category caps do apply — PMI limits how many PDUs certain activities can contribute in a cycle, and those limits change from time to time. Before planning a cycle around any single activity, check the current numbers in PMI's CCR Handbook, linked in our sources.

richText: If you earn your PDUs free, renewal costs $60 as a PMI member or $150 as a non-member — every three years, or roughly $20 to $50 a year. That's genuinely modest. If you buy a PDU package instead, you can easily add several hundred dollars per cycle for something you could largely have obtained for nothing. items.question: How many PDUs do you need to renew the PMP?
items.answerRichText: 60 PDUs every three years, with a minimum of 8 in each of the three PMI Talent Triangle areas — Ways of Working, Power Skills, and Business Acumen. That's about 20 hours a year, or roughly two hours a month.

items.question: How much does PMP renewal cost?
answerRichText: The renewal fee is $60 for PMI members and $150 for non-members, every three years. The PDUs themselves need not cost anything, since much learning and all giving-back activity can be free — so the true cost can be as little as $20 a year. See our

items.question: Can you earn PDUs for free?
items.answerRichText: Yes, and most people can cover a large share of a cycle at no cost. Working in your certified role counts as giving back, and free webinars, chapter events, mentoring, teaching, volunteering, and qualifying self-directed learning all count. Just check PMI's current category caps before relying on any one activity.

items.question: What happens if your PMP expires?
items.answerRichText: PMI suspends the certification when a cycle ends without enough PDUs, and if it isn't resolved the credential lapses — after which regaining it means sitting the exam again. That's why logging PDUs as you go matters more than the total looks like it should.
